In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Ma'arij

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A questioner asked for a punishment about to befall﴾

It is well known that the verb *sa'ala* (سَألَ, "to ask") does not take the preposition *bi* (بِ) in the way it does here. For this reason Ibn Kathir said: the verb is used in the sense of another verb that takes *bi*, a verb that is implied: *mā istaʿjala* ("what he hastened for"). He supported this with His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ (Al-'Ankabut 29:53). It is also reported from Mujahid (d. 104 AH) that *sa'ala* means *da'a* ("to call upon").

He supported this with the words of the disbelievers quoted in His saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:32). Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) also mentioned this view from Mujahid.

It was also read as *sāla* (سالَ, "to flow") without the hamza, from *al-sayl* (السَّيْل, "flood"). Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir mentioned this reading and said: it is a valley in Hell. It was also said that it is a lightened form of *sa'ala*. End of quotation.

Perhaps what supports the view of Ibn Jarir is that the verb is used in the sense of another similar expression, His saying: ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it﴾ (Al-Shura 42:18), and so on.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had already explained this meaning when discussing His saying: ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky"﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:32). He referred to the Surah of *Sa'ala* and said: "A further clarification will come, God willing."

He had shown there that their saying indicates their ignorance, since they did not seek guidance toward it if it was indeed the truth.

Since he, may Allah have mercy on him, referred to this Surah for further clarification, the appropriate reading is this verse: ﴿A questioner asked﴾ in the sense of "he hastened" or "he called upon," because of the connection between the verse of *sa'ala* and the verse: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth﴾ mentioned above. The two are linked by the occasion of revelation.

[Page 265]

As Ibn Jarir and others reported from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿A questioner asked﴾, he said: "A caller called (for a punishment about to befall)." He said: "It is their saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us…﴾" to the end of the verse. The one who said it was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaldah.

The clarification alluded to can be deduced from this connection, and from his, may Allah have mercy on him, statement that it indicates their ignorance, and from clarifying whether this punishment that is about to befall will occur in this world or on the Day of Resurrection.

What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that the ignorance of the Quraysh is shown by both reason and transmitted evidence. Reason requires the seeking of benefit and the repelling of harm, as it is said:

"The wise one strives for what is beneficial, so do not be one who strives [for what is not]."

As for transmitted evidence: among what Allah related to us is that the magicians of Pharaoh, who came challenging Musa, peace be upon him, to the utmost degree of challenge, when they witnessed the truth, said, "We believe," and they fell down prostrate and did not remain arrogant, as Allah related to us their account in His Book. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So the magicians were cast down prostrate﴾ ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa"﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:120–122). When Pharaoh confronted them and said: ﴿Do you believe in him before I give you permission?﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:71) to the end of his speech, they said, and this is the point of evidence here: ﴿We will never prefer you over what has come to us of clear proofs and over He who created us﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:72). They paid no attention to his threat or his intimidation. They said mockingly: ﴿So decide what you will decide﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:72). When they witnessed the clear proofs, they fell down prostrate and declared their faith, whereas these disbelievers of Quraysh speak this same kind of speech.

As for the occurrence of the punishment that was asked about, it will befall them on the Day of Resurrection. The present tense, which indicates the present, was used to emphasize its certainty, as though it were being witnessed. Al-Fakhr al-Razi (d. 606 AH) said this, and he said: it is similar to His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ (Al-Nahl 16:1).

For the Almighty's words, ﴿To the disbelievers; none can avert it﴾ ﴿from God, Lord of the ascending stairways﴾, there is evidence for the certainty of its occurrence, because what none can avert must necessarily occur. As for when it will occur, the verse of (al-Tur) that is similar to this one shows that it will be on the Day of Resurrection, in His words: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur﴾ ﴿none can avert it﴾ [al-Tur: 7-8]. Then He explained the time of its occurrence: ﴿On the Day the sky will sway violently﴾ ﴿and the mountains will move swiftly﴾ [al-Tur: 9-10]. And in the context of this surah, in His words: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass﴾ ﴿and the mountains will be like wool, fluffed up﴾ ﴿and no intimate friend will ask after his intimate friend﴾ ﴿they will be made to see one another﴾, up to His words: ﴿calling out to one who turned his back and withdrew﴾ ﴿and gathered [wealth] and hoarded it﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 8-18]; all of these are among the conditions of the Day of Resurrection, and thereby the time of its occurrence is indicated.

Perhaps in His words, ﴿calling out to one who turned his back and withdrew﴾ ﴿and gathered [wealth] and hoarded it﴾, there is a response to those who made light of the punishment and sought to hasten it, repaying them in kind, just as they called for it and asked for it for themselves in mockery. So it calls them to itself as a rebuke and a warning, in answer to their call with a call. That is: if you called for the punishment in the world, then this is the punishment calling you to it. ﴿Calling out to one who turned his back﴾ from hearing the call, and turned away from it and withdrew. This response, with these attributes preceding it, of the sky changing like molten brass, the mountains moving like wool, and the severing of family ties out of terror and dread that unsettle hearts, is what actually happened in the world, as al-Qurtubi mentioned the story of Jubayr ibn Mut'im.

He said: "I came to Madinah to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the captives of Badr, and I heard him reciting: ﴿By the Mount [Tur]﴾ ﴿and a Book inscribed﴾, up to His words: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur﴾ ﴿none can avert it﴾ [al-Tur: 1-8]. My heart was nearly split, and I embraced Islam, out of fear of the punishment descending; I had not thought I would rise from my place before the punishment came."

Al-Qurtubi also mentioned, from Hisham ibn Hassan, who said: "Malik ibn Dinar and I set out to al-Hasan, and with him was a man reciting (al-Tur) until he reached: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely occur﴾. Al-Hasan wept, and his companions wept, and Malik began to tremble until he fainted."

Ibn Kathir mentioned, from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), that one night he was patrolling Madinah when he heard a man reciting (al-Tur); he was so affected by it that he was ill for twenty nights, and he was visited during his illness. Thus this frightening description was a response to that mocking request. And Allah knows best. We hope we have fulfilled the clarification that he intended, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 70, verse 4:

The words of the Most High: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾.

In this noble verse, the measure of this day is fifty thousand years. Other verses have come stating that it is a thousand years, in the words of the Most High: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count﴾ [al-Hajj: 47], and His words: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him in a Day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ [as-Sajdah: 5] (p-267). Thus there is a difference between them in measure by a factor of fifty.

The Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him) examined this question in his book Daf' Iham al-Idtirab (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction), and in Adwa' al-Bayan in Surah al-Hajj, at his discussion of the Most High's words: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord﴾ up to the end of the verse [al-Hajj: 47].

It should be noted that the days are different: in (Sa'ala) it is the day of the ascent of the Spirit and the angels, and in Surah as-Sajdah it is the day of the ascent of the command; so there is no contradiction.

The commentary on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when the sky will be like molten brass﴾

Al-Muhl (المهل): the dregs of oil (durdiyy al-zayt). It has also been said to mean other things.

The Shaykh, may God's mercy be upon us and upon him, has already discussed this in Surah al-Rahman, when commenting on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when the sky splits open and becomes rose-red like red leather﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 37].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 70, verse 9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the mountains will be like wool(al-ihn)﴾

Al-ihn (wool, a term for dyed or carded wool): it is wool. In another verse the description of al-ihn as "fluffed" appears, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when the people will be like scattered moths, and the mountains will be like fluffed wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 4-5]. Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 70, verse 10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And no intimate friend will ask an intimate friend﴾

Al-ḥamīm (intimate friend, close companion): the relative, the close friend, and the loyal ally, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Repel evil with that which is better; then indeed, the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 34].

In this noble verse: on the Day of Resurrection, no intimate friend will ask an intimate friend, even though they will be made to see one another. Almighty Allah has explained the reason for this, which is that each person will be preoccupied with himself, as in His saying, exalted is He: (p-268) ﴿For every man among them, on that Day, there will be a matter that will occupy him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 37]. Each one flees from the other, saying: "Myself, myself," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother, ﴿and his mother and his father, ﴿and his spouse and his children﴾ [ʿAbasa: 34–37].

Something even greater than this has been reported in the hadith of intercession: every prophet says, "Myself, myself." And there came His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 2]. Beyond that terror there will be none except for the believers: ﴿and they will be safe from terror on that Day﴾ [al-Naml: 89]. May Allah, exalted is He, make us among them. Āmīn.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 70, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious (haluʿan)﴾

Al-Halu'" (haluʿ, "anxious" or "prone to distress") is on the pattern fa'ul, derived from al-hala' (haluʿ, "anxiety"), and is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah, the form expressing intensity). As for al-hala', al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: it is the extreme speed of impatience and distress upon contact with what is disliked, and the extreme speed of withholding upon contact with good. Allah explained it in the verse: ﴿When evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he is withholding﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:20–21].

The word "al-insan" (mankind) here is singular in form, but it is intended as a genus, meaning the human species in general. The evidence for this is the exception that follows in His saying: ﴿except those who pray﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:22]. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-'Asr 103:1–3], and its parallels are many.

Ibn Jarir said that this description of anxiety applies to the disbelievers. Two matters support what he said:

The first: its explanation in the verse, and the exception of those who pray and what follows it from it, because all those attributes are among the characteristics of the believers. For this reason He followed it concerning them with His saying: ﴿Those will be in gardens, honoured﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:35]. Its implication is that those excepted from it are in contrast to that.

The second: the authentic hadith: "How wonderful is the affair of the believer! All of his affairs are good. If hardship befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him; and if ease befalls him, he is grateful, and that is good for him. This is not the case for anyone except the believer." Its implication is that non-believers are the opposite of that, and it is they to whom the description mentioned in the verse applies: that he is anxious (haluʿ).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 70, verse 22:

The saying of the Most High: ﴿Except those who perform prayer,﴾ ﴿who are constant in their prayer.﴾

Allah, the Most High, described those He excepted from the restless man (al-halu'a) with nine attributes:

(p-269) Two of them are specific to prayer, namely the first and the last. This indicates the importance of prayer and the obligation of great earnestness in attending to it. This is among the established matters in the religion, because of its station in Islam. In their description here as: ﴿who are constant in their prayer﴾, and at the end: ﴿who guard their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 34].

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "Constancy in it (al-dawam) is persistence in performing it; they do not neglect it, nor do they occupy themselves away from it with any of the distractions."

He mentioned the hadith of Aisha, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The most beloved of deeds to Allah are those that are most constant, even if they are few."

What he said is supported by the saying of the Most High: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; glorifying Him therein in the mornings and the evenings. Men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah and establishing prayer and giving zakah, fearing a Day⦆ [al-Nur: 36-37], and His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Jumu'ah, then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9].

He said: Guarding it (al-muhafazah) means that they observe the thorough performance of ablution for it and its appointed times, they establish its pillars, and they complete it with its sunnahs and its etiquettes. This is supported by the saying of the Most High: ﴿Certainly will the believers have succeeded, who are during their prayer humbly submissive﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1-2].

And the hadith of the one who prayed poorly, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Return and pray, for you have not prayed." He negated that he had prayed, despite his performing the prayer before him, because he did not guard it by fulfilling its rights.

Allah began and ended those excepted with prayer, which indicates that prayer is the root of every good and the starting point of all that is mentioned, because of His saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer. And indeed, it is difficult except for the humbly submissive﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45]. So it is a help toward every good.

And because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45], it is a barrier against every wrong. Thus it combines the two ends of the legal objective: help toward good and protection from evil, that is, bringing about benefits and repelling harms. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) gave it his utmost care, as is known, to the extent that he made it the distinguishing line between Islam and disbelief in his saying (ﷺ): "The covenant between us and them is the prayer; whoever abandons it has disbelieved." 

(p-270) The scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, agreed on killing the one who abandons it. The speech of the scholars on the effect of prayer upon the heart, soul and feelings of the believer, and what it brings him of tranquility and ease, is very extensive; all of its meanings are suggested by the meanings of Surah al-Fatihah.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 70, verse 24 (part 1 of 5):

﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right﴾ ﴿for the beggar and the deprived﴾

This is the second attribute, and it corresponds to paying the zakat (obligatory almsgiving). The "known right" can only refer to what is obligatory, and this is the view of most exegetes. That the surah is Meccan does not preclude this, for the basic legislation may have been established in Makkah and the details revealed in Madinah, in the second year after the Hijrah. Here there is a general statement in this verse.

The first point: "in wealth." The second: "the known right," meaning the prescribed amount that is paid out. No verse details this general statement except ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], and the Sunnah has explained this general statement.

As for "wealth," because it is in the form of an annexed noun (idafah), it encompasses all their wealth, but the matter is not so. The zakatable wealth is only a part of the whole. Its categories, according to all Muslims, are:

First: the two monetary metals, gold and silver.

Second: what comes out of the earth, such as grains and fruits.

Third: trade goods.

Fourth: livestock, which has its conditions and thresholds (anṣibā', sing. niṣāb, the minimum threshold). Each of these four has its details, and in the first three there is some disagreement.

The Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on us and on him) had already presented everything related to their rulings, in general and in detail, under the two verses ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34] and His saying ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 141]. The zakat on livestock and the zakat al-fitr (the charity of fast-breaking) have not previously been mentioned. Accordingly, we present a portion of that here, to detail the threshold in each of them, what is due upon the threshold, and the matters that the need calls for mentioning, such as mixing of property (khullah), for example, the attributes of the one who pays zakat, and the preferred opinion where there is disagreement. Then we follow this with a comparison between these thresholds in the cattle and the thresholds for gold and silver, to show the strength of the interconnection between them all and the precision of the Lawgiver in measurement.

First: explaining the type of livestock subject to zakat.

Know, may Allah have mercy on us and on you, that the position of the majority is that there is no zakat on livestock except on the three categories of grazing animals: camels, cattle, and sheep and goats, with sheep and goats being equal. Water buffalo are attached to cattle. Camels include both the Arab camels and the Bactrian camels. The disagreement concerns horses.

For Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him), his evidence: he argued for the obligation of zakat on horses by analogy with the other three categories, when they are kept for breeding, that is, when they are both males and females, in contrast to when they are all males, with the common factor being reproduction in each. He also stipulated that they must be pasture-grazing (sa'imah).

And by the hadith: "There is no owner of gold who does not pay its zakat, except that on the Day of Resurrection plates of fire will be made for him, and his forehead, side and back will be branded with them," and so on. In it is mention of all the zakatable wealth: camels, cattle, and sheep. They said: "And horses, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Horses are of three kinds: for one man they are a reward, for another a shield, and for another a burden. As for the one for whom they are a reward: a man who tethers them in the way of Allah and lengthens their tether in a meadow or a garden..." up to the end of what came in this section. "And a man who tethers them out of self-sufficiency and chastity, then does not forget Allah's right in their necks or their backs, they are for him a shield. And a man who tethers them for show and for enmity toward the people of Islam, they are for him a burden."

He (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Allah's right in their necks and backs is zakat. His two companions, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, disagreed with him in this, and Zufar agreed with him. And by what al-Daraqutni, al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib narrated from the hadith of Jabir, raised (to the Prophet): "On every pasture-grazing horse, a dinar or ten dirhams."

The evidence of the majority for the absence of obligation regarding them, and the response to the evidence of Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him):

The majority cited the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no zakat on a Muslim's slave or his horse."

The horse (faras) is a generic noun that encompasses all horses. Also, it was not mentioned along with the other categories until he (ﷺ) was asked about it. If it were similar to them in ruling, he would not have omitted it in mention.

And the hadith: "I have pardoned you regarding horses, so give the zakat on silver (riqqah)." Narrated by Abu Dawud.

They answered Abu Hanifah's argument by saying that Allah's right in their necks and backs is lending them out and providing them to others when they are requested.

They also answered the hadith of Jabir with what al-Shawkani and al-Daraqutni reported: that it is not a valid proof.

Abu Hanifah responded to the majority's evidence: that "his horse" is general, and he holds the hadith applies when the horse is for service. As for when horses are for breeding, analogy has specified them. As for the hadith "I have pardoned you regarding horses," he said it is not authentic. This is a claim that requires proof, for al-Shawkani mentioned that it is sound (hasan).

Perhaps what refutes Abu Hanifah's evidence is the hadith itself on which he relied, through the contextual indication of the division, since it ties the reward regarding them to striving (jihad) with them, and does not mention zakat. Yet zakat may be more binding than the reward, or more general than jihad, because it applies to one who cannot strive, such as a woman, for example, who pays zakat. Had zakat been upon them, it would not have been excluded from the category of reward.

Second: if Allah's right in the mentioned items were zakat, it would not have been left merely to being remembered, with fear of exposure to forgetfulness. For the zakat on the other three categories was not left for that reason; rather, its owner is pursued for it, the collector comes and takes it, and if its owner refuses, it is taken from him by force. By this the preponderance of the majority's position of non-obligation becomes clear.

On another side, there has been divergence of statements from Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him) regarding how horses are treated and what is paid as their zakat. It is said that he gave the choice between paying one dinar or ten dirhams for each horse, or valuing them and paying five dirhams for every two hundred dirhams.

The Hanafis (al-Ahnaf) made the zakat on horses a matter for their owners, with the collector having no role in it, and the ruler not compelling them to pay it. He elaborated on this at length in al-Hidayah. Perhaps the best that can be said on this is what came from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) in the Sunan of al-Daraqutni. He said: Some people from the Levant came to Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "We have acquired wealth, horses and slaves, and we wish to purify them." He said: "What my two companions did before me, I will do." Then he consulted the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: "It is good." Ali remained silent, so he asked him, and he said: "It is good, provided it is not a regular jizyah (poll tax) that they will be held to after you." So he took ten dirhams from each horse. And in it: he placed a dinar on each horse.

In al-Muntaqa, from Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him), they said: "We wish that there be for us in them zakat and purification." So it is, therefore, circling between recommendation and abandonment.

It has also come in the same long hadith mentioned above that they said: "And donkeys, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Nothing has been revealed to me concerning them except this comprehensive and unique verse: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾" [al-Zalzalah: 7]. Narrated by the six (compilers) except al-Tirmidhi.

Accordingly, the texts that are explicit either for obligation or for abandonment are not suitable as proof. The hadith that has a possible meaning regarding "Allah's right in their backs and necks" was described by Ibn Abd al-Barr as general (mujmal), so there was no textual support in the explicit prophetic reports for the Hanafis' position on the obligation of zakat on horses. What remains is the implication of the hadith and the statement of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him).

As for the implication of the hadith, we have already pointed out the contextual indications in it for non-obligation.

As for the action of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), there are also indications in it, indeed evidence, for non-obligation, namely:

First: they were the ones who asked him to pay it and purify them with zakat, and the imposition of zakat does not depend on the desire of the owner.

Second: Umar's hesitation and his not taking it from them the first time. Had it been known to him as zakatable, it would not have been hidden from him, nor would he have hesitated.

Third: his declaration that his two companions had not done it before him, so how could he do it?!

Fourth: Ali's statement: "provided it is not (a jizyah) after you." That is: if Umar took it in response to their desire, there is no harm, since they volunteered it, as long as that does not become a cause for making it binding upon others, so that it would become like the jizyah imposed on Muslims.

Among what is cited as evidence for the majority is the hadith: "I have pardoned you regarding horses and slaves, so pay the zakat on your wealth." Narrated by Abu Dawud.

Al-Shawkani said, with a sound chain (isnad): This agrees with the hadith: "There is no (zakat) on a Muslim's horse or his slave," narrated by the group.

The Hanafis answered Umar's hesitation by saying: horses were not known to the Arabs as pasture-grazing for breeding, but they appeared after the conquests, in the time of Umar. In this statement there is room for examination. Accordingly, there is no evidence for the obligation of zakat on horses, so it remains under the original exemption. For this reason, horses are not mentioned in the book on the thresholds of grazing animals. It is not an objection to this that cattle are also not mentioned in it, because the zakat on cattle has come in several texts in the books of the Sunan.

Al-Bukhari and others explain the thresholds of zakat and what is taken in it. It is known that no explicit text from the Book of Allah details this, but it was already stated in the introduction of the Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on us and on him) that among the types of explanation is the explanation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah, and this is a kind of the explanation of the Qur'an, based on His saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7].

The Sunnah has explained the pillars of Islam, such as the number of units of prayer (rak'ahs), the times of the prayers in detail, and the rites of Hajj.

Likewise, the Sunnah explained the general statement about this right, and in what types of wealth it is due. The most comprehensive text in this regard is the document of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he wrote and attached to his sword. Abu Bakr and Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) acted upon it, and the practice continued upon it afterward.

The group narrated it from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "He said: Abu Bakr sent me a document, and the engraving on the seal was: 'Muhammad' in one line, 'Messenger' in one line, and 'Allah' in one line:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. This is the obligatory charity which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made obligatory upon the Muslims, and which Allah commanded His Messenger to give. Whoever among the Muslims is asked for it in its proper form, let him give it. And whoever is asked for more than that, let him not give it: For every twenty-four camels or fewer, for every five, a sheep. When they reach twenty-five up to thirty-five, there is a bint makhad (a female camel in its second year). If there is no bint makhad, then an ibn labun (a male camel in its third year). When they reach thirty-six up to forty-five, there is a bint labun (a female camel in its third year). When they reach forty-six up to sixty, there is a hiqqah (a female camel in its fourth year) suitable for the stallion. When they reach sixty-one up to seventy-five, there is a jadha'ah (a female camel in its fifth year). When they reach seventy-six up to ninety (p-275), there are two bint labun. When they reach ninety-one up to one hundred and twenty, there are two hiqqah suitable for the stallion. When they exceed one hundred and twenty, then for every forty there is a bint labun, and for every fifty a hiqqah. Whoever has only four camels, there is no charity due on them unless their owner wishes. When they reach five, there is one sheep.

As for the zakat of sheep in their pasture: when they are forty up to one hundred and twenty, there is one sheep. When they exceed one hundred and twenty up to two hundred, there are two sheep. When they exceed two hundred up to three hundred, there are three sheep. When they exceed three hundred, then for every hundred there is one sheep.

If a man's pasture-grazing sheep are fewer than forty, by one, there is no charity on them unless their owner wishes. Flocks shall not be combined, nor separated, out of fear of the charity. Whatever belongs to two partners, they shall settle between them equally." (The hadith is given in full.)

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 70, verse 24 (part 2 of 5):

So the Prophet (ﷺ) clarified in this book the shares (anṣibah, sing. niṣāb) of camels and sheep and what is obligatory in each of them, but he did not address the shares of cattle. However, the shares of cattle were clarified by the hadith of Mu'adh in the books of the Sunan (the compilers of the Sunan).

He said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded me when he sent me to Yemen that I should not take anything from the cattle until they reach thirty. When they reach thirty, then in them is a young bull (tabi') or a young cow (tabi'ah) in its second year, until they reach forty. When they reach forty, then in them is a cow in its third year (musinnah)."

With these two authentic texts, the explanation of the shares of the grazing livestock (bahīmat al-an'ām) is complete: camels, cattle and sheep. This is the position of the majority of scholars (al-jumhūr), and it is the practice (al-'amal) upon which the community has acted.

As for what is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: "For every ten cattle, a sheep, up to thirty, and then in them is a tabi'," no one has acted upon it.

* *

Note.

There is no zakat on the waqs (the intermediate amount between two nisab thresholds) in the grazing livestock. The waqs is the amount between each nisab and the one that follows it, such as between five and nine camels, between one hundred and twenty and one hundred and twenty-one sheep, and between thirty and forty cattle. This is agreed upon, except that the Hanafis differ regarding the waqs of cattle only. The correct view is the position of the majority in all cases, based on the hadith of Mu'adh and the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "until they reach forty; when they reach forty, then in them is a musinnah." Its implicit meaning (mafhūm) is that there is no zakat after thirty until they reach forty, so there is no zakat in what lies between thirty and forty.

Abu Hanifa says that in this range there is a proportional part of the tabi'. He made the zakat on grazing livestock conditional upon being reproductive (naslan) and pasturing freely (sawman), and held that there is no zakat on fodder-fed animals (ma'lūfah) or animals used for work, such as camels used for carrying loads and cattle used for ploughing, and the like.

Malik said: there is zakat on fodder-fed animals and on working animals. He said in the Muwatta' the following: "On the camels used for drawing water (nawāḍiḥ), the cattle used for irrigation (sawāqi), and the cattle used for ploughing: I am of the view that zakat should be taken from all of them when zakat is due on them."

The proponents of Malik's view argued for it on two grounds:

The first: from the texts.

The second: from the rational meaning (ma'nā).

As for the texts: what came in general terms in the hadith of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) concerning the shares of zakat, namely that for twenty-four camels and below, sheep are due, one sheep for every five, applies in its generality to both pasturing and fodder-fed animals. This is for camels. Likewise for sheep: one sheep for every forty sheep, meaning without the condition of pasturing.

As for the rational meaning: al-Baji said that if the quantity of expenses affects zakat, then it affects its lightening and burdening, and does not affect its removal or establishment, as in mixing (khultah), separation (tafriqah), watering, irrigation with a water-wheel (naḍḥ), and the like. There is no difference between pasturing and fodder-fed animals except the lightness or heaviness of the expense. As for the ability to benefit from them, it is on one standard, and feeding them does not prevent milk or offspring.

The majority also responded to Malik's evidence on two grounds:

The first: from the texts.

The second: from the rational meaning.

As for the texts: what came concerning camels in the hadith of Bahz ibn Hakim, in which it says: "For every forty camels, a pasturing one (sā'imah), a bint labūn." Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others.

Concerning sheep, there is the hadith: "On pasturing sheep is zakat," and it is an authentic hadith.

In the letter of Abu Bakr and Umar, the condition of pasturing came in both hadiths, while Malik's evidence is unrestricted (muṭlaq). The unrestricted is to be understood in light of the restricted (muqayyad), as is well known.

Among what indicates the preference of the majority's evidence is that in the hadith on sheep, the unrestricted wording concerning the number, "one sheep for every forty sheep," serves to define the nisab more than to define the attribute. And the hadith "On pasturing sheep is zakat" serves to define the place of obligation more than to define the number. From another angle, the two hadiths are to be regarded as complementary, and each of them is general in one respect and specific in another. The hadith "On pasturing sheep is zakat" is general concerning sheep without a number, and specific to pasturing. The hadith "For every forty sheep, one sheep" is general concerning sheep, and specific to forty. So the generality of each is specified by the particularity of the other. It is said: "On pasturing sheep is zakat when they reach forty," and it is said: "For every forty sheep, one sheep, when they are pasturing." By this, the evidences harmonize regarding camels and sheep, through the stipulation of pasturing and the fixing of the number.

As for cattle: consensus (ijmā') has been reported on the requirement of pasturing. Among the majority's evidences from the rational meaning is that pasturing and breeding are for growth, so they admit of compassion (muwāsāh), whereas fodder-fed animals and working animals do not admit of compassion. From what has preceded, the majority's position on the requirement of pasturing and breeding is preferred. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

What has come concerning the khultah (mixing), which is the mixing of two properties together for two or more persons. It is of two kinds:

First: khultat a'yān (mixing of substances).

Second: khultat awṣāf (mixing of attributes).

Khultat a'yān is when the property is held in common among the co-owners (khulaṭā') by way of undivided shares (mushā'), such as those who inherited sheep or cattle, for example, and did not divide them, or they were given as a gift and they did not divide them. In this mixing, the ruling on the property is the same as if it belonged to one person.

Khultat awṣāf is when the property is distinct, and each of them knows his share and his property by number and attributes, whether by its colours, by its brands (wasm), or the like. However, they mixed the property so that its management would be easier, as in their mixing in the herder, the pasture, the place of grazing and the place of shelter, the stallion, the water-bucket (dalw) and the milking place (maḥlab), and what is similar to that which has been stated, because of what it contains of ease, and the sufficiency of one of each of these for all the property. If it were separated, each property would need one of each of these things. This mixing has an effect on zakat according to the three imams: Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on them). It has no effect according to Abu (p-278) Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him). The effect, according to him, is only in undivided mixing (khultat al-mushā').

Those who hold that it affects zakat differed over whom it affects:

Ahmad and al-Shafi'i said: it affects all the co-owners, those who own a nisab and those who do not.

Malik said: it affects only those who own a nisab or more, and for those who do not own a nisab, there is no effect on them.

The majority's evidence against Abu Hanifa regarding its effect is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying in the book clarifying the shares of charity: ("Nothing that is together is to be separated, and nothing that is separated is to be joined, out of fear of the charity. Whatever belongs to two partners (khalītayn), they settle between themselves equally.")

The majority said: the prohibition on separating what is together can only apply to mixing of attributes, because mixing of undivided shares cannot be separated out of fear of the charity. Likewise, "they settle equally" is said only regarding mixing of attributes, because what is taken from undivided shares is taken from the whole and also in undivided form, since each partner in an undivided share has his share of every sheep in undivided form.

The example for all of this, according to all, is as follows: If three persons each own forty sheep, then if each of them is on his own, each one owes one sheep. If they mix, they owe together one sheep, shared equally among them, because their total is one hundred and twenty, which is the limit for one sheep.

This is the view of the three imams who hold that mixing has an effect: Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad. If the first has twenty sheep, the second forty, and the third sixty, then there is also one sheep due on them.

But according to Ahmad and al-Shafi'i, each pays according to his share. If the sheep were valued at sixty dirhams, the first would owe ten dirhams in proportion to his sheep out of the total, the second twenty, and the third thirty; each in proportion to his sheep out of the total.

According to Malik: nothing is due from the first, because he did not own a nisab. The sheep is due from the second and third only, in proportion to their sheep out of the total. So the second owes two-fifths of the value, which is twenty-four, and the third owes three-fifths of it, which is thirty-six dirhams, and so on.

The evidence is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Nothing that is together is to be separated, and nothing that is separated is to be joined, out of fear of the charity. Whatever belongs to two partners, they settle between themselves equally."

The majority said: the prohibition on separating what is together, and the division between them equally, is evidence that mixing has an effect on zakat, because of the relief it brings.

Al-Baji said: as in the relief regarding irrigation of the field, what is watered by the water-wheel (naḍḥ) and what is watered without it.

Abu Hanifa said: "what belongs to two partners" means the two associates, but his saying (ﷺ) "they settle equally" refutes this, because settling equally is only realized in mixing of neighbourhood and attributes.

Malik said: mixing has no effect on whoever does not own the nisab, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "For every forty sheep, one sheep." Whoever does not own forty sheep owes no zakat, and mixing has no effect on him. Perhaps, from the texts presented, the preferred view is that of Ahmad and al-Shafi'i concerning the question of mixing. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The conditions that have an effect on mixing, according to those who hold it, are as follows. According to Ahmad (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him), there are five attributes, namely the unity of the two properties in: the pasture; the grazing place; the place of shelter; the milking place; the stallion.

According to al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him), al-Nawawi mentioned ten attributes: the first five, and he added: that the two partners should be among the people of zakat; that the mixed property should be a nisab; that a full lunar year should pass over them; the unity of the watering place; the unity of the herder.

According to Malik: the herder, the stallion, the place of shelter, and the water-bucket. By the water-bucket is meant the watering place according to al-Shafi'i. On this basis, all of them are approximately in agreement regarding the attributes. What al-Shafi'i added is known in the Law, because they are conditions for the basic obligation of zakat. But they differed over what is meant by these attributes: must all of them be required, or is the presence of some of them sufficient?

The reality is that there is no explicit text on this. Rather, the matter returns to the investigation of the underlying cause (taḥqīq al-manāṭ) regarding what brings about the relief. Malik suffices with some of them, such as the stallion, the pasture and the herder. Al-Shafi'i required the presence of all those attributes, failing which the mixing does not have an effect. Each of them has disagreements within his school concerning those attributes, which we will not prolong by tracing in detail. What concerns us is clarifying the preferred view on what is disputed regarding the basic question. It has become clear that the preferred view is the following:

First: the validity of the effect of mixing.

Second: the requirement of those attributes by which mixing is realized according to custom.

A remark.

We have come to know the shares of the grazing livestock in summary and in detail, and there remains for us the answer to a question that has long occupied the thoughts of every student of it, which is what all the jurists say: the measures are tawqīfī (fixed by revelation), and among them are the shares of zakat. The meaning of tawqīfī is that there is no room for independent reasoning (ijtihād) in them. But is it that they came without an underlying rationale, or is there among these shares a relationship and a consistent proportion?

The reality is that although the obligation upon every Muslim, and what Muslims have held both in the past and in the present, is compliance and obedience, nevertheless, since we live in a materialistic age, in which the economic system is the basis of the policy of the world today, some may aspire to an answer to this question.

I have tried to answer it by making a general comparison in which a consistent proportion exists, as follows:

First: in the two precious metals. It is known that the nisab of gold is twenty mithqals, and of silver two hundred dirhams, and in each of them is one-fortieth (rub' al-'ushr). The exchange rate of the dinar was ten dirhams, so the nisab of gold, by multiplying twenty by ten, equals two hundred. This is a consistent proportion, as you see.

When we come to the proportion between gold and silver, which is the basis of currencies, and between sheep, we find the following:

**First**, regarding the hadith of ʿUrwa al-Bariqi: the Prophet ﷺ gave him a dinar to buy a sheep for them. He went and came back with a sheep and a dinar. The Prophet ﷺ said to him, "What did you do?" He said, "I bought two sheep for the dinar. Then a man met me and said, 'Will you sell me a sheep?' So I sold him one sheep for a dinar." The Prophet ﷺ said to him, "May Allah bless you in the transaction of your right hand."

The meaning of this is that the purchasing value of the dinar equals two sheep. Multiply twenty dinars by two and it equals forty sheep, and this is the *nisab* (the minimum threshold) of sheep. In forty sheep there is one sheep, and its purchasing value is half a dinar, which is five dirhams, and this is what is taken for twenty *mithqal* (a unit of weight). Thus the ratio also holds consistently between gold and silver and sheep.

As for the ratio between sheep and camels: we find that a camel (*badana*) is equivalent to seven sheep in the sacrificial offering (*hady*). The *nisab* of camels is five, and multiplying it by seven gives thirty-five. If it were made six, it would equal forty-two. So we take the lesser figure, out of caution for the right of the poor. Thus there is a consistent ratio between the *nisab* of camels and the *nisab* of sheep.

Likewise, the *nisab* of sheep and the *nisab* of the two precious metals have a consistent ratio. Thus precision and the consistency of the ratio in the thresholds are made manifest.

**What may and may not be taken in zakat.**

The scholars agree that male animals are not taken in zakat, except for *ibn labun* (a male camel in its third year) for one who does not have a *bint makhad* (a female camel in its second year).

They differed regarding the case where the entire *nisab* consists of males, though in reality this is rare. However, they agreed that *sikhal* (young kids or lambs) are not taken, while the reckoning of them is obligatory upon their owner.

As came from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Count them with the young one that the shepherd brings, and do not take it from them." It is not permissible to take the stallion camel, the he-goat, the *rubba* (a ewe with young), or the milch animal, because of the harm this causes to the owner of the property.

Likewise the *sakhla* (young animal) and the *ajfa* (lean animal) are not taken, because of the harm to the poor. The basis for this is what Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated in the *Muwatta*, saying: "Count them with the young one that the shepherd carries, and do not take it, nor take the *akula* (fattened animal), nor the *rubba*, nor the *makhid* (a pregnant ewe), nor the stallion of sheep. Take the *jadhaʿa* (a six-month-old) and the *thaniyya* (a year-old)." This is a *ʿadl* (median) between the lesser and the best of the flock. The "lesser" of the flock is its young, and "the best" is its old and fattest; so it is *ʿadl*, that is, the middle.

Here a word must be emphasised. Every financial system in the world is a purely material system that rests on figures and statistics. It is dry in its form, like a body without a soul. Except for the system of zakat, which is a living system with its own spirit and compassion.

At the time when it obliges the wealthy to pay a portion to the poor, it forbids the collector to take beyond what is due, or the best of what he finds, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Beware of the choicest of their property."

And at the time when the wealthy person pays a part of his wealth, he feels that he pays it for the sake of Allah and awaits His reward, may He be exalted. Thus zakat became between a collector who is scrupulous and a property owner who is voluntarily giving. The collector fears the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Beware the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and Allah." And the owner hopes for ten times its like, and seven hundred, and multiplied increase beyond that for a good deed.

There occurred an astonishing incident which no financial system in the world has ever witnessed: "The collector of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out for *sadaqa* (charity), and passed by a man in a village near Madina who owned camels. He counted them and said to the owner, 'Bring out a *bint labun* (a female camel in its third year).' The owner of the camels said, 'How can I bring out a *bint labun* in zakat when she has no back to ride nor udder to milk? Rather, here is a fat she-camel, take her in the way of Allah.' The collector said, 'How can I take something that is not due from you?' They quarrelled together, the collector and the owner of the property, and then they took [the matter further]. The collector said to him, 'If you are determined, here is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ near you in Madina. Go with her to him; if he accepts her from you, I will take her.' He went with her, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him, 'Is it from a good heart?' He said, 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' So he ordered the collector to take her, and he ﷺ supplicated for blessing for him. So he lived until the time of Muʿawiya." So the zakat of this man's camels was the very spirit of zakat in Islam, unlike what the owners of property do in other systems.

As for the system of taxes, where people evade, minimise, and keep multiple ledgers, some of which are for the tax authorities, in which one understates one's income and earnings so that the tax burden may be lighter, because one sees it as a penalty like the *jizya* (poll tax); and others are kept for oneself, so that one may know the true reality of one's wealth.

As for zakat: its owner offers his zakat for the sake of Allah, in order to purify his wealth, according to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾ [al-Tawba: 103].

And as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed one of you gives a charity, and it falls first into the palm of the Most Merciful, and He causes it to grow for him just as one of you raises his *falu* (foal) — that is, the young of his horse — until it becomes like Mount Uhud."

(p-٢٨٣) And as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Charity does not diminish wealth."

**Zakat al-Fitr (the charity of breaking the fast).**

The most important topics of zakat al-Fitr are the following:

First: its ruling and the origin of its legislation.
Second: upon whom it is due.
Third: from what it is given.
Fourth: how much it is.
Fifth: when it is due.
Sixth: whether value (*qiyma*) may be paid in it or not.

And likewise the value in the other types of zakat.

As for its ruling: it is an individual obligation (*fardh ʿayn*) according to Ahmad and al-Shafiʿi. According to Abu Hanifa it is *wajib* (obligatory) in his terminology, that is, what is made obligatory by the Sunna.

According to the Malikis it is obligatory, and it has been said it is a Sunna.

Khalil ibn Ishaq said in his *Mukhtasar*: "The *sáʿ* is made obligatory by the Sunna…" etc.

The reason for their disagreement is whether it falls within the general scope of: ﴿And give zakat﴾ [al-Baqara: 43], meaning it was legislated by the original legislation of zakat in the Book and the Sunna, or whether it was legislated by a separate independent text.

Whoever says it is an obligation (*fard*) says it falls within the general command to give zakat. Whoever says it is *wajib* — this is the terminology of the Hanafis. The matter does not differ in the outcome of the obligation, except that according to them one does not become a disbeliever by denying it.

The Malikis said: "The *sáʿ* of wheat is made obligatory by the Sunna," etc. That is, its obligation is by the Sunna and not by the Book.

And according to them: the people of a town are not fought over withholding it, but whoever denies its legislation is killed. This is the difference between them and the Hanafis.

However, in the wording of Malik in the *Muwatta* there is an unrestricted use of *wujub*, for he said: "The best I have heard concerning what is obligatory upon a man in zakat al-Fitr is that a man pays it on behalf of everyone whose maintenance he is responsible for," etc.

Among the causes of disagreement among the Imams, may Allah have mercy on them, are the texts of the Sunna. Among them is their saying: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made zakat al-Fitr obligatory, a *sáʿ* of dates or a *sáʿ* of barley," and the hadith continues.

The word *faraḍa* (made obligatory): those who say it is obligatory took it so, and others took it in the sense of "determined" (*qaddara*), because *fard* means measure and decisiveness.

The hadith of Qays ibn Saʿd ibn ʿUbada in al-Nasaʾi says: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered us to give the charity of breaking the fast before zakat was revealed. When zakat was revealed, he did not command us nor forbid us, and we continued doing it."

Whoever says it is *wujub* and *fard* says: the command of the first is for obligation, and the obligation of the zakat of wealth encompassed it by its generality. Thus no new command was needed with it, and it was not abrogated so as to be forbidden, and it remained under its first obligation. And the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made zakat al-Fitr obligatory as a purification for the fasting person from idle talk and obscenity, and as food for the poor. Whoever pays it before the prayer, it is an accepted zakat; and whoever pays it after the prayer, it is an ordinary charity among charities." Whoever does not say it is obligatory says: it is a purification for the fasting person and food for the poor, so it is for a cause tied to it, and it lapses with the lapse of its time; and if it were an obligation it would not have lapsed with the passing of its time. The others replied that this is by way of encouraging hastening to pay it, and there is no barrier to its being an obligation and also a purification.

What supports this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾ [al-Tawba: 103]. So it is an obligation and it is a purification. The preponderant view in all of this is that it is an obligation, because of the wording of the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ made zakat al-Fitr obligatory, a *sáʿ* of dates." For the word *faraḍa*, if it is used absolutely, indicates obligation; and if it means "determined," then the obligation comes from the general verses on zakat, and this is stronger.

And the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ addressed us and commanded the charity of breaking the fast, a *sáʿ* of dates," etc. Narrated by Abu Dawud. The command indicates obligation, and there is no diverting indicator here.

(p-٢٨٥) Al-Nawawi said: the view that it is obligatory is the view of the majority of scholars, and this is the view by which one's duty is discharged, and by which the servant is freed from responsibility. And Allah, may He be exalted, knows best.

As for from what it is given: the basis for this is the narration of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, which Malik narrated in the *Muwatta* from him. He said: "We used to give a *sáʿ* of food, or a *sáʿ* of *aqit* (dried cheese), or a *sáʿ* of barley, or a *sáʿ* of dates, or a *sáʿ* of raisins."

The word *sult* came, and the word *daqiq* (flour) came, and the word *sawiq* (roasted grain flour) came. A group stopped at what was explicitly stated only, namely the Zahiriyya. The majority looked to the generality of "food" and the purpose of its legislation, with differences in detail among the Imams, may Allah have mercy on them, as follows:

First: according to the Shafiʿis it is permissible to give it from every staple food, based on the narration of Abu Saʿid, in which the word *taʿam* (food) occurs.

Second: from the usual staple of the person obligated to pay it, because it is the surplus over his own sustenance.

Third: from the usual staple of the town, because it is a right that is due upon the person and relates to food, like expiation (*kaffara*).

Al-Nawawi said: it is permissible from every grain that is subject to *ʿushr* (tithe). And regarding *aqit* there is a difference of opinion among the Shafiʿis and Malikis.

Malik narrated the hadith of Abu Saʿid mentioned above in the *Muwatta*. Al-Baji said in his commentary: it is given from the staple food. And it is reported from Malik in the *Mukhtasar*: one pays it from everything for which zakat is due, if it is from one's staple food. This is like the view of al-Nawawi: from every grain subject to *ʿushr*. Al-Baji discussed the question of whether it is valid from rice, maize, and millet. He said: it is not valid from them according to Ashhab, and it is valid according to Malik. Al-Qattani discussed chickpeas, lupin, and lathyrus, and said: Malik permits them if they are one's staple; Ibn Habib does not permit them, because they are not among the explicitly stated items.

The position of the Malikis agrees that a foodstuff which is added to something else, like spices — coriander, cumin, and the like — is not valid.

The Hanbalis: Ibn Qudama said in *al-Mughni*: from every grain and fruit that is used as a staple.

And he said in *al-Sharh*: that is, when the explicitly stated kinds are absent, so every staple of grains and fruits is valid.

(p-٢٨٦) He said: and the apparent meaning of this is that a staple other than these is not valid for him, such as meat and milk. And when these also are absent, he gives what takes the place of the explicitly stated kinds.

And from Ibn Hamid among them: even fish meat and livestock meat. And they do not refer it to the nearest staple of the cities. Dried cheese is valid for the people of the desert if it is their staple. And among them: whoever is able to give the explicitly stated item and gives something else, it does not suffice him.

The Hanafis: it is permissible from wheat, dates, barley, raisins, roasted grain flour, and flour. And from bread, with consideration of its value. And according to them, value may be given as a substitute for all of them, with differences among them regarding the amount due from these kinds, between a *sáʿ* or half a *sáʿ*, as will come, God willing.

Ibn Qudama discussed them in *al-Mughni* at his saying: "Whoever gives the value, it does not suffice him." It is reported from Ahmad: "I fear it does not suffice him, contrary to the Sunna of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." And with this exposition we find that the Imams, may Allah have mercy on them, agreed upon what is explicitly stated in the narration of Abu Saʿid. Some of them added, from what is not explicitly stated, items that are not explicitly stated — either by the generality of the word "food," even though it is customarily used to mean wheat, yet the consideration is the generality of the expression, which is the linguistic usage; or by the generality of the meaning of the general purpose. The disagreement concerns *aqit*, and the text decides it.

Al-Ahnaf alone held the view that payment of value (al-qimah) is permissible, and they looked to the general meaning of the purpose of zakat, which is his ﷺ saying: "A feast for the poor and a purification for the fasting person." And his saying: "Enrich them with it so they need not beg." We find here an indication of the permissibility of giving it from everything that serves as food for the poor, and we do not limit it to a particular measure or restrict it to a specific category. Therefore, extending the non-stated to the stated by the common effective cause (jami' al-'illah, the shared underlying reason) is well-founded. As for value, the author of Fath al-Qadir, the commentary on al-Hidayah, discussed this question in the chapter on zakat on wealth, and the core of their evidences is as follows:

First: the exchange of a jadha'ah and a musinnah in camels for two sheep.

Second: the saying of Mu'adh to the people of Yemen: "Bring me a khamis or a labis in place of maize and barley; it is easier for you, and better for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Narrated by al-Bukhari.

(p-287) Third: "The Prophet (ﷺ) saw a fine she-camel among the camels of the zakat, and said: 'What is this?' The owner of the zakat said: 'I bought it back for two camels from the lesser camels.' He said: 'Yes.'"

Fourth: it is like the jizyah; the required amount is taken from it just as its specific item is taken.

The response to all of this is as follows. As for the substitution between a jadha'ah and a musinnah or a hiqqah, and so on, in camels, for two sheep or twenty dirhams, this is what is stated in the hadith of Anas in the earlier Book of Shares, and its text reads: "Whoever is due the zakat of a jadha'ah but does not have it, and has a hiqqah, then the hiqqah is accepted from him, and he adds with it two sheep or twenty dirhams. And whoever is due the zakat of a hiqqah but does not have it, and has only a jadha'ah, then it is accepted from him, and the collector gives him twenty dirhams or two sheep. And whoever is due the zakat of a hiqqah but does not have it, and has only a bint labun, then a bint labun is accepted from him, and he gives two sheep or twenty dirhams." To the end of the hadith.

There is no evidence in this for accepting value in zakat al-fitr, because the text of the hadith concerns one who is obligated to a specific age-category of camel, does not have it, and has one that is higher or lower. For justice between the owner and the poor, the difference is made so that no wrong is done, and it does not depart from the original principle. It does not involve taking value independently; rather it involves taking what exists and then making up the deficiency.

So, had value by itself been sufficient, he ﷺ would have stated it explicitly.

This procedure is permitted only when the required item is absent, and when the required kinds of zakat al-fitr are unavailable, it is possible to move to what exists from the same genus, not to value. This is clear.

Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Fath: "If value were intended, it would vary according to time and place; but it is a legislated measure."

As for the saying of Mu'adh to the people of Yemen, "Bring me a khamis or a labis in place of maize and barley," Ibn Hajar discussed it in al-Fath from the standpoint of both chain and meaning. However, the chain is established. As for its meaning, it was said that it concerns the jizyah.

This was rejected: since it says "in place of maize and barley," and the jizyah is not of these.

(p-288) It was also said: after he receives the obligatory zakat in its kinds, he exchanges it as a sale and mutual exchange, acting on what serves the interest of both parties.

It was also said: it was his own ijtihad, but it was the ijtihad of one of the most knowledgeable of them in what is lawful and unlawful, and so on.

The correct view is the second: that it is a disposal after receipt and after the zakat has reached its place, especially with its transfer to Madinah; this differs from zakat al-fitr, which is not transferred in the first place. Moreover, the scope of zakat on wealth is broader than that of zakat al-fitr, for it includes gold and silver and livestock.

As for zakat al-fitr, it is food for the poor on the day of Fitr, so it is not analogized to them.

As for the fine she-camel he saw ﷺ, and that it was a substitute for two camels, this belongs to the category of exchanging one kind for the same kind for the sake of interest, and it did not depart from the genus of what was obligatory.

As for the jizyah, from which the required amount is taken: there is no evidence in it, since zakat al-fitr has an element of worship (ta'abbud) and connection to a pillar of Islam.

As for the jizyah: it is a penalty upon the people of dhimmah, "by means of submission while they are humbled." Whatever is taken from them fulfils the purpose. Thus no sound basis remains for those who argue for value in zakat al-fitr, let alone the absence of a textual statement on it.

In conclusion: the saying that value is permissible contradicts the principles from two aspects.

The first aspect: when the Prophet ﷺ mentioned those categories, he did not mention value with them. Had it been permissible, he would have mentioned it along with what he mentioned, just as he mentioned the substitute in camel zakat; and he ﷺ is the most compassionate and merciful toward the poor of any person.

The second aspect, which is the general rule: one does not move to the substitute except when the original is absent, and whatever branch returns to nullify its root is itself void.

Likewise, Ibn Daqiq al-'Id refuted the Hanbalis' saying that ashnan (a plant-based cleanser) suffices in place of earth in the case of a dog's licking a vessel. That is, because it is not of its genus, and the act is invalid.

Similarly, if all people adopted paying value, the acts involving the stipulated genera would be rendered inoperative,

(p-289) so the branch, which is value, would return to nullify its root, which is food, and thus it is void.

Like what some people say today regarding the hady at Mina, that it is "an equivalent for an equivalent," while it is known that the Hanafis do not permit value in hady, because hady has an element of worship, which is the rite.

It may also be said to them: zakat al-fitr too has an element of worship; it is a purification for the fasting person and food for the poor. Just as the process of buying it, measuring it and presenting it carries an indication of this act of worship. As for presenting it in cash, there is no difference from any other charity in terms of the sense of obligation and the feeling of feeding.

We have extended the discussion of this question at length, because the saying that value is permissible in it emboldened people toward what is greater: the saying that value is permissible in hady, which no one has said without qualification, not even the Hanafis.

Clarifying the required amount in zakat al-fitr

All agree that the obligation in zakat al-fitr on each person for himself is a sa' by the sa' of the Prophet ﷺ, from all the categories mentioned earlier.

Abu Hanifah differed regarding wheat, saying that half a sa' of it suffices. The preferred view on this will be explained, if Allah wills.

Then they differed regarding the weight of the required sa'. The majority said it is five and a third raṭls. Abu Hanifah said it is eight raṭls, and Abu Yusuf opposed him and agreed with the majority. As for the measure of the sa', it is by custom a volume measure, which is four handfuls with the two palms of a man of moderate hands; and because people differ in this, the scholars resorted to specifying its quantity by weight.

Al-Nawawi noted that the measure by weight is approximate, because measured goods differ in weight, heavy and light, according to their kinds, such as lentils and barley for example; and what is customarily measured by volume cannot be precisely controlled by weight, but only approximately.

For this reason the author of al-Mughni said: whoever pays zakat by weight should add an amount that is known to equal the measure, especially if the weighed item is heavy.

(p-290) It is reported from Ahmad that whoever gives the weight of a heavy item by that of a light one has certainly given the obligation with assurance.

* *

The views of the scholars on the weight of the sa'.

The majority said: it is five and a third raṭls, the raṭl being the Iraqi raṭl.

Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is eight raṭls, and Abu Yusuf opposed him as mentioned. The cause of the disagreement is that Abu Hanifah took the saying of Anas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed ablution with a mudd," which is two raṭls, and it is known that the sa' is four mudds; accordingly it would be eight raṭls.

The majority's evidence is that the basis for volume is the custom of Madinah, just as the basis for weight is the custom of Makkah; and the custom of Madinah regarding the sa' of the Prophet ﷺ is that it is five and a third raṭls. This came from Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, who said: "I took the sa' from Abu al-Nadr," and Abu al-Nadr said: "I took it from Abu Dhu'ayb," and he said: "This is the sa' of the Prophet ﷺ known in Madinah."

Abu 'Abd Allah said: we took lentils and measured with them, for it is the most suitable thing we found to measure with, since it does not shift from its place; so we measured with it, then weighed it, and it was five and a third raṭls. He said: this is the most suitable we found, and what became clear to us of the sa' of the Prophet ﷺ.

And if the sa' is five and a third raṭls of wheat and lentils, which are the heaviest grains, then whatever else is among the kinds of zakat al-fitr is lighter than them; so if five and a third raṭls of them is given, it is more than a sa'.

Al-Nawawi said: al-Hafiz 'Abd al-Haqq in his Kitab al-Ahkam reported from Abu Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Hazm that he said: "We found that none of the people of Madinah differ among themselves that the mudd of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with which he paid the charities is not more than a raṭl and a half, nor less than a raṭl and a quarter."

Some said: it is a raṭl and a third, and said: this is not a disagreement, but it is according to its razn, that is, its weight and heaviness, of wheat, dates and barley. He said: the sa' of Ibn Abi Dhu'ayb is five and a third raṭls, (p-291) and it is the sa' of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Among the evidences of the majority, and the reason for Abu Yusuf's return from Abu Hanifah's view, is what came in al-Mughni and elsewhere: when Abu Yusuf came to Madinah and asked them about the sa', they said: five and a third raṭls. He demanded proof from them, and they said: tomorrow. The next day seventy elders came, each one holding a sa' under his cloak, and said: "My sa' I inherited from my father, and my father inherited it from my grandfather," until they reached the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Yusuf began comparing them and found them all equal. They took one of them and checked it against lentils (al-mash, unhusked lentils), and it was five and a third raṭls; so he returned to the view of the people of Madinah.

In that same account: he returned to Iraq and said to them: "I have brought you new knowledge: the sa' is five and a third raṭls." They said to him: "You have opposed the shaykh of the people." He said: "I found a matter for which I had no means of refutation."

As for the weight of the Iraqi raṭl, the basis of unit in it is the dirham. Al-Nawawi reported three views about it:

The first: it is one hundred and thirty dirhams by the dirhams of Islam.

The second: it is one hundred and twenty-eight.

The third: it is one hundred and twenty-eight dirhams and four-sevenths of a dirham, which is ninety mithqals.

In al-Mughni it says: they added a mithqal to it so it became ninety-one mithqals, and by it one hundred and thirty dirhams was completed; they intended by this addition to remove the fraction of the dirham.

Then he said: "and the first practice" (al-'amal al-awwal).

As for the rest of the raṭls in other regions, then as follows, quoted from Kashshaf al-Qina':

The Ba'li raṭl: nine hundred dirhams.

The Qudsi: eight hundred.

The Halabi: seven hundred and twenty.

The Dimashqi: six hundred.

The Misri: one hundred and forty-four. And every raṭl is twelve ounces in all lands, the dirhams being divided by them.

On this basis: the sa' equals six hundred and eighty-five and five-sevenths of a dirham, and four hundred and eighty mithqals.

On this basis also, the sa' in the other raṭls is: in the Misri raṭl, four raṭls, nine ounces and one-seventh of an ounce; in the Dimashqi, one raṭl and five-sevenths of an ounce; in the Halabi, eleven raṭls and three-sevenths of an ounce; and in the Qudsi, ten ounces and two-sevenths of an ounce.

Now, since the world's weights have today been converted to French measures, namely kilograms, and a kilogram is a thousand grams, it is necessary to state the ratio in grams. The matter is this: measures of volume differ in weight and density. I took the sa' that I have and first calibrated it against another, old sa'. On comparison I found a striking matter: the sa' I have exceeds the other by the amount of a handful (qadr mal' al-kaff). I then looked, and the opening (fatha) of the two sa's was different, because the opening of one of the two sa's is wider. Thus the part raised above its opening forms a triangle whose base is longer than the base of the triangle above the other sa'. I therefore calibrated them a second time at the level of the opening only, without any excess, and they were equal. I then calibrated them by water, since water's weight does not generally vary as long as it is potable and not salty, and since it does not allow an extra amount above the rim. After this confirmation, the weight of the sa' was: with crushed lentils, 2,600 kilograms and six hundred grams.

And with water, 3,100: three kilograms and one hundred grams.

I hope this work is sufficient to clarify the approximate weight of the Prophetic sa' in zakat.
